newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR boss says no plans for new Turkish Kurd camp.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR boss says no plans for new Turkish Kurd camp.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said on Tuesday her agency had no plans to open a new camp for Turkish Kurds in northern Iraq as chances of it being taken over by "political and military elements" were very high.

Sadako Ogata said that the agency could not assist the Kurdish refugees in the Atrush camp -- which Turkey says is a base for independence-seeking Kurdish guerrillas -- as long as they remained under the sway of military and political leaders.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees closed down its aid operations last month in Atrush camp, where up to 14,000 people who fled the Kurdish conflict in southeast Turkey in 1994 remain in tents and makeshift huts.

"We can't protect Atrush as such, and we have decided not to set up another camp of this type because chances of it being taken over by the political and military elements of the camp is very high," Ogata told Reuters in an interview.
The UNHCR withdrew from Atrush in January, saying Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas were blocking its operations.
Ogata said Shamsul Bari, UNHCR's director of the northern African and Middle East region, was in northern Iraq negotiating with leaders of the refugees in Atrush camp.
She said camp leaders had asked the UNHCR to continue its assistance and perhaps move to another area where they would be more comfortable.
"But we can't do that," she said. "It's a very dangerous area there. We're not in the camp. They chased us out."
Earlier, UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said that Bari had been slated to meet Massoud Barzani, head of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), the faction which controls the area.
"As of now, we still haven't any movement out of the camps," O'Toole told a news briefing.
A UNHCR source later confirmed Bari held talks with Barzani on Sunday in Salahuddin "in the context of general consultations and an exchange of views".
This month, the UNHCR said it would not remove its flag over the camp as a symbol of international protection for refugees, but Ogata complained that her agency had no access to them.
"De facto, we cannot protect people unless they're free. Unless we can effectively exercise our protection mandate, we shouldn't really have the flag up there," Ogata said.

Atrush, 60 km (40 miles) from the Turkish border, was set up in 1994 for Kurds fleeing into northern Iraq from southeast Turkey, where villagers are caught in the middle of a dirty guerrilla war between Turkish troops and the PKK.
More than 21,000 people have died in the 12-year-old war.
UNHCR says it is ready to assist refugees wishing to go home or those wishing to stay in northern Iraq at temporary sites.

The Atrush affair has touched off sensitivies with Turkey, which has repeatedly called on UNHCR to pull out of the camp. Turkey's defence minister Turhan Tayan said last week that the camp was "a nest of terror".
